name: John Newton
title: John Newton: Amazing Grace and a repentance that had to mature
description: John Newton, the origin of Amazing Grace and his past in the slave trade: a story of grace that calls for memory and responsibility.

sections.heading: A song and a past that must not be erased
paragraphs: John Newton is remembered as a pastor and the author of Amazing Grace. Before that, he had taken part in the transatlantic trade in enslaved people and became captain of a ship engaged in that traffic. The National Portrait Gallery keeps both sides of his life: the clergyman and the man involved in a brutal business.

His religious change did not bring about an immediate public denunciation of that whole system. In 1788 he published Thoughts on the African Slave Trade and worked with William Wilberforce in the abolitionist cause. An honest biography must keep that gap in time and the harm done in view, even while recognizing his later opposition to the trade.

sections.heading: The hymn was born in a real community
paragraphs: The Cowper & Newton Museum connects the hymn with the New Year’s service of 1773 in Olney. The evidence includes Newton’s diary and sermon notes. The text was published in Olney Hymns in 1779, in a collection prepared with William Cowper. It was not born as an on-the-spot account of a shipwreck.

That morning’s sermon was based on 1 Chronicles 17:16–17. The museum explains that the theme invited people to look back on life with gratitude and to consider the future. This information places the song within pastoral work and keeps its origin from being reduced to a dramatic scene repeated without checking.

reflection: Luke 3:8–14 calls for fruit in keeping with repentance and applies that demand to specific behavior. Newton’s story can be read in light of that responsibility: acknowledging the grace we have received means learning to call evil by its name. The memory of a conversion must not erase those who suffered from the convert’s earlier actions.

For the church, the account invites us to examine the gap that sometimes exists between a profession of faith and its ethical consequences. Change requires acknowledging harm, abandoning unjust practices and seeking the good of others. Grace is proclaimed more honestly when the truth about sin is kept, rather than prettified to build an admirable biography.
review_note: Song lyrics are not reproduced, and the 1748 conversion is not treated as an immediate abandonment of the slave trade. The harm done to enslaved people is kept in view.
